drills.q: Name the OWASP Top 10:2025 categories A01 through A05 in order.
drills.a: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures (new), A04 Cryptographic Failures, A05 Injection.

drills.q: Which 2021 category no longer exists as its own entry in 2025, and where did it go?
drills.a: SSRF, which was A10:2021, folded into A01:2025 Broken Access Control.

drills.q: Give the time-based blind SQLi sleep function for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQL Server.
drills.a: PostgreSQL: pg_sleep(5). MySQL: SLEEP(5). SQL Server: WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'. Oracle typically uses dbms_pipe.receive_message.

drills.q: List the four Django/SQLAlchemy escape hatches you would grep for in a SQLi audit.
drills.a: Django: .raw(), .extra(), RawSQL(). SQLAlchemy: session.execute(text(f'...')) without bindparams. Add Hibernate HQL concatenation for the Java side (CWE-564).

drills.q: A code review shows cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY %s', (col,)). Is it injectable? Is it correct?
drills.a: Not injectable, and not correct. It binds a string constant, producing ORDER BY 'created_at', which sorts by a constant and silently returns unsorted rows with no error. Bind parameters can only occupy value positions because the plan is built at Parse time before Bind. Fix with a server-controlled allowlist mapping the user key to a column, plus a two-value direction map, composed with sql.Identifier().

drills.q: An endpoint returns 200 for every request, but its p50 latency is clustered at 5.02s, 10.04s, and 15.03s. Diagnose and give the same-day mitigations.
drills.a: Time-based blind SQL injection using pg_sleep / SLEEP / WAITFOR. Same-day mitigations, none of which are the fix: set a server-side statement_timeout of ~2s so the sleeps fail fast, rate-limit the unauthenticated route, and block the pattern at the edge. The remediation is finding the concatenated query and parameterizing it. Do not let the mitigation close the remediation ticket.

drills.q: Explain second-order SQL injection with a two-step example, and say which tool class misses it.
drills.a: Step 1: INSERT INTO users (username) VALUES (%s) with the value admin'-- , parameterized and safe; it is stored as literal text. Step 2, months later, a report job runs f"SELECT * FROM audit WHERE username = '{row['username']}'", producing ... WHERE username = 'admin'--'. SAST usually misses it because it taints the HTTP request object and stops at the INSERT. IAST catches some of it at runtime on exercised paths. The durable control is a CI rule banning string-formatted SQL everywhere, not just near request handlers.

drills.q: Someone proposes validating the ORDER BY column with the regex ^[a-z_]+$ instead of an allowlist. What does that fail to stop?
drills.a: Authorization bypass. ORDER BY password_hash passes that regex. Combined with a paging endpoint the sort becomes a boolean oracle you can binary-search to extract the column. An allowlist is not about character classes, it is about which columns the SERVER has decided are sortable.

drills.q: Your team wants to build the IN clause as 'WHERE id IN (' + ','.join(map(str, ids)) + ')'. What is the safe form and what else does it fix?
drills.a: Use 'WHERE id = ANY(%s)' with a real Python list on Postgres, or one placeholder per element. Beyond removing the injection, it also gives the planner a single stable statement to cache instead of a new query text for every list length, which stops prepared-statement cache churn on high-cardinality lists.

drills.q: Why is prompt injection categorically different from SQL injection, and what follows from that for defense?
drills.a: Every working injection defense uses two transport channels so the interpreter never re-parses data as grammar: Parse/Bind for SQL, argv for shells, DOM APIs for HTML. A transformer has one token stream, so system prompt, user turn, retrieved chunk, and tool output are attended to identically. There is no bind parameter for attention. It follows that the defense is containment rather than prevention: least-privilege tools enforced at the gateway, no high-risk tool in the same turn as an untrusted read, per-agent identity, budgets, and human gates on irreversible actions.

drills.q: A vendor's pentest report says 'no OWASP Top 10 findings.' What do you conclude, and what do you ask for instead?
drills.a: Almost nothing about security, and something about scope. The Top 10 covers 248 CWEs out of 968 in MITRE's dictionary; A01 alone is 40 CWEs at a measured 3.73% incidence, which is a floor set by what scanners can find. Business logic, tenant isolation, and multi-step authenticated state are usually out of scope and are where the expensive incidents live. Ask for the test scope, whether authenticated multi-role testing was performed, and coverage against ASVS L2. The Top 10 is an awareness document; ASVS is the requirements standard.

drills.q: You inherit a monolith with 60 open injection findings and one engineer-month. Sequence the work and defend the sequence.
drills.a: Triage by reachability and privilege, not scanner severity: unauthenticated routes and high-privilege DB roles first. Week one, ship the two systemic controls that cap the entire population at once: drop the app DB role to least privilege (converts every finding from 'read everything' to 'read what this service owns') and suppress DB error propagation (kills error-based extraction across all 60). Add the CI rule as ERROR with a shrinking grandfather allowlist so the count cannot grow. Then fix by clusters, because 60 findings usually come from 5 or 6 helper functions. Then add tests asserting sort order and tenant scoping so the fixes cannot silently regress.

drills.q: Design the security posture for a production agent with tool access, then say which two controls you would ship first with one week.
drills.a: Gateway-enforced tool allowlist rather than a prompt instruction, per-agent identity with short-lived scoped credentials (ASI03), no high-risk tool available in the same turn as a read of untrusted external content, human confirmation on irreversible actions (send, delete, pay, deploy), hard step count plus wall-clock timeout plus token and cost budget (LLM10 / ASI08), full prompt-to-action traces, and treating every model output as untrusted input to whatever consumes it (LLM05). With one week: the gateway-enforced tool allowlist and the step-plus-cost budget. Both are days of work, both are enforced outside the model so injection cannot argue with them, and they bound the two failure modes that end careers: irreversible actions and runaway cost. Per-agent identity is highest value and slowest, so it is a quarter item.

drills.q: CVE-2026-42208 hit your LiteLLM deployment. You have patched to 1.83.7-stable. Are you done? Justify.
drills.a: No. It was a PRE-AUTHENTICATION SQL injection on the key-verification path, reachable from every LLM route with no credentials, and observed exploitation used UNION payloads against LiteLLM_VerificationToken, litellm_credentials, and litellm_config. You must assume every upstream provider key the proxy held was read: rotate all of them, audit provider-side usage logs across the full exposure window (exploitation began within 36 hours of advisory indexing, so the window may predate your detection), and then change the architecture so the gateway does not hold every provider credential in the same database it queries before authenticating anyone.

drills.q: Argue the counter-position: ORMs and modern frameworks have made SQLi a solved problem not worth senior interview time. Where is that right and where is it wrong?
drills.a: Right about greenfield application code written entirely through the ORM's typed query API, where the framework parameterizes by construction. Wrong about the seams, which is where every real finding lives: identifier positions the ORM must emit from user input (Django CVE-2024-42005 used a JSONField key as a column alias), raw-SQL escape hatches, second-order paths where DB reads are treated as trusted, stored procedures using EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, analytics query builders, and every gateway and admin tool in the dependency tree. CVE-2026-42208 was written in 2026 by people who knew what SQL injection was. The senior framing is that prevention is achievable for new code and containment (least-privilege DB role, error suppression, egress deny) is what actually bounds the damage everywhere else.
